Atelectasis

Failure of all or part of the lung to expand due to loss of air in the alveoli

Lobar collapse refers to collapse of a particular lobe of the lung

Lung collapse is collapse of whole lung

Must be differentiated from consolidation

Signs of volume loss on chest x ray

Displacement of mediastinum and trachea towards the collapsed lung

Elevation of the hemidiaphragm

Compensatory hyper inflation of adjacent lobes or opposite lung

Causes of atelectasis

Consolidation (in pneumonia)

Bronchial obstruction by : tumor inside bronchi or compressing from outside, mucus plugging of major airways, inhaled foreign bodies, iatrogenic (et tube inserted too far)

Surfactant problems (ARDS)

Inflammatory etiologies

Lung fibrosis

RUL Collapse

Right upper lobe collapses upward and medially, the horizontal fissure get pulled up by collapsed lobe

RUL will appear as Thickened paratracheal tissue

Signs of volume loss on chest x ray

Displacement of mediastinum and trachea towards the collapsed lung

Elevation of the hemidiaphragm

Compensatory hyper inflation of adjacent lobes or opposite lung

Alma Jula, Matti Waris, Kalle Kantola, Ville Peltola, Maria Söderlund-Venermo, Klaus Hedman, and Olli Ruuskanen, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Middle lobe collapse

Collapsed middle lobe sits next to the right heart border and appear as increase in density leading to loss of the right heart border on the x ray (silhouette sign)

Signs of volume loss

Mediastinal/ tracheal shift

Elevation of the hemidiaphragm

Compensatory hyperinflation

Mikael Häggström, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons · Stillwaterising, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

RLL Collapse

Right lower lobe collapses inferiorly and medially and appear as a triangular hyper density referred to as the sail sign

There is loss of the definition of the right hemidiaphragm

Right heart border stay visible and not obscured

Right hilum gets pulled down by the collapsed lobe

Signs of volume loss

Mediastinal/ tracheal shift

Elevation of the hemidiaphragm

Compensatory hyperinflation

Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

LLL Collapse

Left lower lobe collapses inferiorly and medially and appear as a triangular hyperdense area behind the heart, it is called retrocardiac sail sign

There is loss of the definition of the left hemidiaphragm and the descending aorta

left heart border stay visible and not obscured

Left hilum gets pulled down by the collapsed lobe

Signs of volume loss

Mediastinal/ tracheal shift

Elevation of the hemidiaphragm

Compensatory hyperinflation

Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

LLL is tricky to detect because collapses behind the heart

Normally, you can see some pulmonary vessels through the heart, if they are not seen then put LLL in your DDx

O'Dea, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

LUL Collapse

Left upper lobe collapses inward and upward producing increase in density in most of the left lung field

Loss of definition of left heart border and left mediastinum

Left hemidiaphragm is not obscured

LUL collapse

Left lung hilum gets pulled upward by the collapsed lobe

There is lucent outline over aortic arch called luftsichel sign

Signs of volume loss

Mediastinal/ tracheal shift

Elevation of the hemidiaphragm

Compensatory hyperinflation

Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Lung Collapse

Collapse of entire lung, shown as increase density all over the lung field of the affected lung

Signs of volume loss

Mediastinal/ tracheal shift

Elevation of the hemidiaphragm

Compensatory hyperinflation
